analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals, insurers, labs, and pharmacy middlemen to publish real prices and disclose hidden rebates and ownership.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved it 49–0 with 88 bipartisan cosponsors, but it never received a floor vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force hospitals to post their standard charges — including the discounted cash price and the rates they negotiated with insurers — in a single free, machine-readable file, with penalties reaching $5 million a year for large hospitals that don't comply. It would require health insurers to give patients a real-time tool showing what a service will cost them out of pocket, and to publish their in-network rates every three months. It would also force pharmacy benefit managers (the companies that negotiate drug prices for employers and insurers) to reveal the rebates and fees they collect and keep, ban "spread pricing" in Medicaid, and make big hospital systems and private-equity-owned medical practices report who owns them and how they're merging. Finally, it would extend funding for community health centers, teaching health centers, and the National Health Service Corps.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and the employers and unions that buy health coverage gain the ability to see actual prices before getting care, instead of opaque estimates. Employers and plan sponsors gain detailed reports on the rebates PBMs receive from drug makers and how much PBMs keep. Taxpayers gain visibility into hospital consolidation and Medicare Advantage billing practices. Low-income and rural patients benefit from continued funding for community health centers, teaching health centers, and the National Health Service Corps.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, employers who buy coverage, community health centers

how_it_helps.text: Requires every hospital to publish a free, single machine-readable file of standard charges — gross charges, discounted cash prices, and the negotiated rates with each insurer — plus a plain-language list of at least 300 shoppable services; a hospital can no longer satisfy this with an online price estimator tool after 2024.

Imposes a graduated penalty structure with a $5 million minimum annual fine for larger hospitals that fail to publish the required prices for a continuous year, and directs HHS to maintain a public list of noncompliant hospitals and report enforcement numbers to Congress each year.

Requires health plans to offer a real-time self-service tool showing a patient's actual cost sharing — deductibles, copays, coinsurance, and any prior authorization or step-therapy rules — and to publish their in-network rates and drug payment information every three months in public files.

Bars pharmacy benefit managers and insurers from gag clauses that hide drug rebate information from plan sponsors, and requires annual reports on every drug's rebates, fees, formulary placement, and how much PBM middlemen retained — with civil penalties up to $10,000 per day for failing to report.
Requires pass-through pricing and bans spread pricing — where a PBM charges the state more than it pays the pharmacy and keeps the difference — in Medicaid pharmacy arrangements.

Requires Medicare Advantage insurers to report payments, risk scores, and prior-authorization denials broken down by providers they have an ownership stake in, and makes hospitals, large physician practices, and private-equity or venture-capital-owned medical businesses report ownership, mergers, and debt annually, with a public HHS report on consolidation trends.
Extends funding for the Teaching Health Center Graduate Medical Education program, the Community Health Center program, and the National Health Service Corps.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, health insurers, PBMs, Medicare Advantage insurers, diagnostic labs, and private-equity-owned provider groups bear the compliance costs — building disclosure files, running reporting systems, and facing fines up to $5 million per report for false ownership filings. Some of those costs are likely to show up in premiums and provider prices, though the bill's premise is that visible prices and rebate disclosure will lower total costs more than compliance raises them. The extended community health center and workforce funding is a federal cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, insurers, PBMs, and private-equity-owned providers

drawbacks.text: Compliance is expensive: hospitals must rebuild chargemaster files and insurers must produce three quarterly public rate files, and those administrative costs can be passed through to premiums and billed charges, so some of the transparency burden lands back on consumers in the short run.

The bill relies on disclosure rather than price limits, so it changes incentives without guaranteeing lower prices — published negotiated rates may simply become a floor that providers and insurers converge toward, rather than a source of downward pressure.

The PBM rebate reports go to plan sponsors, not fully to the public: the bill expressly lets insurers and PBMs place reasonable restrictions on public disclosure of the reports, so much of the rebate data would reach employers and regulators but not ordinary shoppers.
Transparency tools have historically been little used by patients directly; the bill's consumer benefit depends on employers and comparison tools actually mining the files.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a serious, enforceable transparency package: it closes the most exploited gaps in the existing hospital and insurer rules (estimator-tool workarounds, gag clauses, spread pricing) and pairs them with real penalties and public enforcement lists. Its costs are real but conventional — compliance spending and some risk of rate convergence — and its biggest design weakness is that much of the PBM data stays out of public view. On balance the benefits to patients and coverage purchasers outweigh the compliance costs, but the bill would have lowered prices only to the extent that employers, states, and market participants actually used the disclosed data.

outcome.mechanism: The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved the bill unanimously 49–0 in May 2023, but it never came up for a vote by the full House; in December 2024 it was referred to a health subcommittee, and the Congress ended without action.

narrative.text: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-WA) and Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ) — the chair and ranking member of the Energy and Commerce Committee — jointly introduced the bill on May 22, 2023, and it was referred to Energy and Commerce plus the Ways and Means and Education and Workforce committees.
The bill drew 88 cosponsors, split 42 of 216 House Democrats and 46 of 224 House Republicans.
On May 24, 2023, the Energy and Commerce Committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported as amended by a 49–0 recorded vote.

Despite clearing committee unanimously, the bill never received a House floor vote; on December 17, 2024, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where it sat until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, health insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers are better off because the bill never became law — they avoid the price publication mandates, rebate disclosures, and spread-pricing ban. Patients, employers, and community health centers got nothing: no published negotiated rates, no PBM rebate reports, and no funding extension.

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly split across parties: 88 cosponsors split 42 Democrats and 46 Republicans, and the committee approved it 49–0 with no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill bans spread pricing in Medicaid, bans rebate gag clauses, and requires PBMs to disclose the rebates and fees they collect and how much they keep, with fines of $10,000 per day for failing to report. PBM revenue from spread pricing and retained rebates comes at the expense of the employers and patients who pay drug claims.

Hospitals must publish negotiated rates and cash prices in free public files — a requirement they have resisted — and face a $5 million-a-year penalty floor for large facilities that fail to comply, plus new billing-identifier requirements for off-campus departments. Hospital chargemaster pricing is the starting point for bills that uninsured and out-of-network patients receive.

Insurers must publish their in-network rates quarterly and build a real-time tool showing each patient's actual cost sharing. Negotiated-rate secrecy is central to how insurers price plans, so disclosure erodes their pricing position.

MA organizations must report risk scores, prior-authorization denials, and payments broken down by providers they own — data aimed at upcoding and self-dealing through physician ownership. This transparency threatens a major profit mechanism in Medicare Advantage.

industries.industry: Private equity and venture capital in health care
industries.note: PE- and VC-owned medical businesses, large practices, and hospitals must report ownership, mergers, debt, and leases annually, with up to $5 million penalties per false or missing report and a public consolidation report. This shines a light on the ownership structures behind rising facility fees and staffing shortages.

industries.industry: Community health centers and teaching health centers
industries.note: The bill extends funding for the Community Health Center program, Teaching Health Center GME, and the National Health Service Corps, which serve uninsured and rural patients directly.
